label: Merge
description: M.C. Taylor's first Merge album loosens the ragged folk of his earlier records into warmer, full-band arrangements with pedal steel and organ. The songs move at an unhurried, breezy pace, with Taylor's rasp working through themes of family and faith. It is the record that carried Hiss Golden Messenger out of the private-press underground and into a wider Americana audience.
lineage: Grows out of the raw, homemade folk of Bad Debt and Haw into a fuller country-rock sound that sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and the Band, which Taylor kept refining on later Merge albums.
key_tracks: Lord, Help The Poor and Needy

label: Merge
description: M.C. Taylor turns worries about work, fatherhood, and getting by into some of his most direct, tuneful songwriting, backed by a road-tested band playing loose, breezy country-soul. Pedal steel, warm harmonies, and rolling grooves carry the songs, sitting between Southern soul and country rock. It suits listeners who want comforting, grown-up roots music with a bit of swing.
lineage: Continues the country-soul direction of Lateness of Dancers; its loose, communal grooves sound indebted to the Band and the Grateful Dead.
key_tracks: Like a Mirror Loves a Hammer

label: Merge
description: A joyful counterpart to Heart Like a Levee's worry, leaning into gospel-tinged uplift and a live-in-the-room band feel. The guitars are warm and interlocked, with less studio polish and loose, rolling tempos. Its songs about hard times and gratitude suit fans of communal, soulful country rock.
lineage: Keeps Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic-country sound loose and communal; the road-band feel sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and the Band.

label: Merge
description: A more expansive record that stretches Hiss Golden Messenger's country-soul into longer, more atmospheric arrangements. Themes of self-doubt, depression, and endurance run through the lyrics, delivered over some of the band's most layered playing. It suits listeners who like their Americana patient, textured, and emotionally frank.
lineage: Expands the Merge-era country-soul sound with a more atmospheric, layered production that sounds akin to the 2010s indie-Americana of peers like Bon Iver's circle.

label: Merge
description: A quieter, more reflective Hiss Golden Messenger record that folds subtle home-studio textures into the band's usual country-soul without losing the pedal steel and warm harmonies. The songs reckon with stillness, isolation, and small-town North Carolina life. It suits listeners who want gentle, unhurried roots music for late evenings.
lineage: Shows Taylor bending his sound, which sounds rooted in the Grateful Dead and the Band, toward home-studio textures while keeping the same cosmic-country core.
key_tracks: Way Back in the Way Back
If It Comes in the Morning

label: Merge
description: A relatively lean, upbeat record with brighter tempos and some of Taylor's most direct choruses. Pedal steel and harmony vocals sit up front, in keeping with the buttery, breezy sound that defines his Merge catalog. It suits fans who want Hiss Golden Messenger at its most sunny and hook-driven.
lineage: A late-period return to a communal, road-band version of Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic country, sounding indebted to the Band and Grateful Dead country rock.

label: Mexican Summer
description: Williamson's Mexican Summer debut sets her plainspoken, drawling voice against loose, twangy full-band arrangements, a step up in scale from her earlier, sparer albums. Songs move between hushed acoustic passages and warmer country-rock breeze, dealing frankly with desire, loneliness, and desert landscapes. It suits listeners who like intimate songwriting with a hazy, wide-open feel.
lineage: Moves Williamson's earlier lo-fi folk toward a fuller country-rock sound that sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon; she later formed Plains with Katie Crutchfield.

label: Mexican Summer
description: A patient, spacious record built around Williamson's low, unhurried voice and finger-picked, pedal-steel-laced arrangements. It trades the rawer edges of Cosmic Wink for a smoother, more mystical take on desert country-rock. Themes of self-possession and desire run through its longer, breezier songs.
lineage: Continues Williamson's Mexican Summer-era cosmic country, which sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and Laurel Canyon; she later formed Plains with Katie Crutchfield.

label: Mexican Summer
description: Williamson's most fully country-identified record, with pedal steel, warm harmonies, and road-song imagery throughout. It works through the end of one relationship and the start of another with plainspoken directness, her voice sitting close and unhurried over two-step and ballad tempos. It suits listeners who want classic country feeling from an indie-bred songwriter.
lineage: Brings Williamson's cosmic-country sound closest to what sounds like Gram Parsons and outlaw-country roots; she also records with Katie Crutchfield as Plains.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: Max Clarke's first full-length as Cut Worms leans on ringing, Everly Brothers-style harmonies and simple, twangy guitar figures played at an unhurried country-pop tempo. It is a warm, sunny record that wears its 1960s and '70s country-rock influences openly without pastiche. Clarke's plainspoken songwriting keeps the mood breezy even when the lyrics turn wistful.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Everly Brothers harmony singing and 1960s country-pop and country-rock, filtered through a Brooklyn DIY-pop sensibility.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: A double album that widens Cut Worms' sound with brighter production and more layered harmonies while keeping the same easy country-pop tempos. Clarke's songwriting stays plain and melodic, closer to classic AM radio than to twang-rock swagger. It is the most expansive record in his catalog.
lineage: Extends the buttery, harmony-driven sound of Hollow Ground, which sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and Laurel Canyon pop, into a longer, more varied set.

label: Jagjaguwar
description: The self-titled album pares Cut Worms' sound back to a leaner, more direct country-pop. Melodies stay bright and hooky, riding on the same twangy, harmony-laden guitar interplay as his earlier work. It reads as a mid-career consolidation rather than a reinvention, for fans of sweet, retro-minded songcraft.
lineage: Keeps Cut Worms in a country-pop vein that sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and Gram Parsons, as across his whole catalog.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Recorded largely alone at home after Morby moved back to Kansas City, this is his most spare, plainspoken record, built on finger-picked guitar, harmonica, and unhurried tempos. It trades the fuller band arrangements of his Los Angeles-era work for a hushed, small-town Midwestern feel. Reviewers linked its plainness to Springsteen's Nebraska as much as to cosmic country.
lineage: A stripped-down turn in Morby's catalog that still carries the breezy, Dead- and Parsons-indebted guitar sensibility of his earlier band records.

label: Dead Oceans
description: Sparked by an old photograph of his father found after a family health scare, this album is a warm, mid-tempo meditation on mortality and memory, built on breezy country-rock arrangements with pedal steel and horns. Recorded partly in Memphis, it draws on that city's soul and gospel history as much as on Laurel Canyon songwriting. It suits listeners who want reflective songs with a big, generous band sound.
lineage: Continues Morby's move toward a fuller folk-rock and country sound that sounds indebted to Dylan, the Band, and Memphis soul; it was followed by the companion More Photographs (A Continuum).

label: Dead Oceans
description: Morby's latest album works in a bucolic folk-rock palette, continuing the warm, unhurried style of This Is a Photograph with an even more pastoral, near-spiritual tone. Pedal steel and acoustic textures dominate over the breezy tempos. It suits listeners who want gentle, open-hearted songwriting.
lineage: Extends Morby's Dead Oceans-era folk-rock songwriting, which sounds indebted to Dylan and cosmic country.

label: ANTI-
description: McCombs' ANTI- debut loosens his usual cryptic songwriting into warm, soulful, mid-tempo arrangements with breezy electric-guitar interplay and light horns. It is one of his most accessible records, closer to yacht-rock smoothness than to the noisier turns of his earlier catalog. Political and personal songs sit side by side without ever raising their voice.
lineage: Pulls McCombs' idiosyncratic songwriting toward a breezier guitar-rock sound that sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead and continues on Tip of the Sphere and Heartmind.

label: ANTI-
description: A more exploratory record than Mangy Love, stretching several songs into long, Dead-like instrumental passages built on interlocking guitar lines. McCombs' deadpan, riddling lyrics stay intact even as the band jams out around them. It suits listeners who like their songwriting patient and their guitar playing unhurried.
lineage: Sounds the most indebted to Grateful Dead-style long-form guitar jamming of any McCombs record, placing it alongside the 2010s cosmic-rock revival.

label: ANTI-
description: This album keeps McCombs' warm, unhurried guitar-rock sound while turning toward more openly emotional lyrics about grief and love. The tempos stay breezy and the arrangements uncluttered, closer to Mangy Love than to Tip of the Sphere's jams. It is for listeners who want his songwriting at its gentlest.
lineage: Continues McCombs' ANTI- era guitar rock; its softer edges sound indebted to classic Laurel Canyon songwriting.

label: Sacred Bones
description: Damon McMahon's Amen Dunes trades earlier lo-fi murk for warmer, more melodic songs built on loping acoustic guitar and a breathy, drawling voice. Tempos stay slow and breezy, closer to hazy folk-rock than to the drone of his earlier records. It suits listeners who like hypnotic, devotional-sounding songs that unfold slowly.
lineage: Moves Amen Dunes toward a hazier guitar-folk sound that sounds indebted to classic rock and Gram Parsons-era country rock.
borderline_note: More psych-folk drone than classic cosmic country, but Josh Terry grouped it with the C6 revival scene.

label: Sacred Bones
description: A more polished, radio-scaled record than Love, mixing McMahon's drawled vocals with warmer production, occasional synths, and mid-tempo grooves that borrow as much from classic rock as from psych-folk. Songs draw obliquely on McMahon's own family history and the pressures of masculinity. It suits listeners who want hypnotic rock with a surfer's easy momentum.
lineage: Extends the breezy, classic-rock-informed direction of Love into a fuller studio sound that sounds akin to the Cosmic American Music revival.
borderline_note: More psych-folk than straight cosmic country; included per Terry's C6 grouping.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Cohen's solo debut after Deerhoof and the Curtains sets warped, subdued psychedelic pop against loose, home-recorded arrangements. Guitars ring and drift rather than solo, and the tempos stay unhurried throughout. It established the mysterious, hazy sound that runs through his later solo work.
lineage: Sounds indebted to breezy Laurel Canyon-style pop songwriting, filtered through a lo-fi, tape-warped production sensibility.

label: Captured Tracks
description: A slightly warmer, more melodic follow-up to Overgrown Path, keeping Cohen's soft-focus psychedelic pop but adding more overt hooks and clearer vocal lines. Tempos remain breezy and the mood mellow throughout. It continues his run of quietly beloved, low-key solo records.
lineage: Refines the hazy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting of Overgrown Path without changing course.

label: Captured Tracks
description: Cohen's self-titled third album keeps his mumbled, half-buried vocal style but opens the arrangements up with more keyboard and synth color. The tempos stay slow and breezy, and the mood remains warm rather than melancholy. It suits listeners who like soft-focus, gently psychedelic pop.
lineage: Continues Cohen's subdued psychedelic pop, which sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon songwriting as much as to the art-pop of his former band Deerhoof.

label: Hardly Art
description: Made with contributions from Jeff Parker and Josh Johnson, this record keeps Cohen's subdued psychedelia while adding jazzier color and understated hooks. It moves through hazy, mysterious moods without ever raising its volume. It marked Cohen's move from Captured Tracks to Hardly Art.
lineage: Extends Cohen's breezy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting into jazzier arrangements, deepening a catalog that has quietly run in parallel to the wider cosmic-country revival.

label: Bella Union
description: Wilson's breakout solo album is a sprawling, hour-long homage to Laurel Canyon songwriting, built on layered acoustic and pedal-steel textures and long, patient guitar passages. Recorded in his own Laurel Canyon studio, it openly revives the Crosby, Stills & Nash and Neil Young sound of the neighborhood's golden age. It suits listeners who want slow-burning, lushly harmonized folk rock.
lineage: Sounds like a conscious recreation of the Laurel Canyon country-rock of CSNY and Neil Young, made in the same neighborhood that produced it.

label: Bella Union
description: A denser, more orchestrated follow-up to Gentle Spirit, adding strings and a wide cast of guests to Wilson's long-form country-rock songs. Extended guitar jams and layered harmonies stretch several tracks well past the six-minute mark. It suits listeners who want maximal, immersive 1970s-style studio rock.
lineage: Expands Gentle Spirit's guitar rock, which sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon and the Grateful Dead, into a more maximalist, string-laden record.

label: Bella Union
description: A more synth-laced, polished record than Wilson's first two albums, though still built around long, winding guitar passages and breezy tempos. Its slicker, 1980s-tinged studio sound leans toward widescreen soft rock. It suits listeners who like lush, headphone-friendly production over rootsy grit.
lineage: Shows Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism absorbing polished synth-rock textures, sounding akin to 1980s Pink Floyd-style studio rock without abandoning its cosmic foundation.

label: BMG
description: This album pulls Wilson's sound closest to straight country, adding fiddle and pedal steel to his usual breezy, long-form guitar writing. It is a warmer, more rootsy record than Rare Birds, closer in spirit to Gentle Spirit. It suits listeners who want country rock with a stoned, unhurried glow.
lineage: Brings Wilson's Laurel Canyon revivalism back toward country rock, sounding indebted to Gram Parsons and Nashville session-style picking.

label: American Recordings
description: Ethan Miller's band follows up their debut with a bigger record of heavy, extended guitar jams built on Crazy Horse-style fuzz and Southern-rock swagger. Songs stretch out into long instrumental sections without losing their anthemic hooks. It suits listeners who want 1970s-scaled hard rock with room to roam.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young & Crazy Horse and the Allman Brothers' long jams; Miller came from the psych band Comets on Fire.
key_tracks: Dancers at the End of Time

label: American Recordings
description: A dense, heavily produced record of sprawling, riff-driven rock songs, several stretching past seven minutes with extended guitar interplay. It leans harder into arena-scaled classic rock than Howlin Rain's earlier records, while keeping the same Dead- and Crazy Horse-indebted jam structure. It suits listeners who want big, road-worn guitar rock.
lineage: Pushes Magnificent Fiend's long-jam sound, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and Southern rock, toward a heavier, more maximalist studio production.

label: Silver Current Records
description: A looser, more organic-sounding record than The Russian Wilds, leaning into warmer, more soulful arrangements. Extended guitar solos still anchor several songs, but the overall feel is breezier and less studio-heavy. It suits listeners who like classic-rock sprawl with a gentler, homespun touch.
lineage: Returns Howlin Rain's jamming, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and the Dead, to a rawer, band-in-a-room feel after the maximalism of The Russian Wilds.

label: Silver Current Records
description: Howlin Rain's long-form rock at its most confident, with harmonized lead guitars, anthemic choruses, and extended solos in the mode of the Dead's live improvisation. Crazy Horse-style fuzz and rolling mid-tempo grooves give the songs a road-worn, 1970s swagger. It suits listeners who want big classic-rock guitar with room to stretch.
lineage: Sounds like a full expression of Grateful Dead- and Crazy Horse-style extended-jam songwriting.

label: Single Lock Records
description: Rae's breakthrough solo debut is warm and searching country-folk. It examines faith, sexuality and family with unusual gentleness and directness.
lineage: Continues Nashville's Cosmic American Music lineage from Parsons and the Flying Burrito Brothers through the Single Lock label's Muscle Shoals-adjacent roster.

label: Single Lock Records
description: A more textured, golden-toned record than Putting On Airs, layering Rae's strong, unhurried voice over arrangements that borrow from 1970s AM radio without tipping into kitsch. Every arrangement stays tasteful and uncluttered, with pedal steel and close harmonies giving it a breezy, cosmic-country glow. It suits listeners who want warm, soft-focus country-folk.
lineage: Extends Rae's Nashville country-folk into a sound akin to 1970s AM-radio soft rock and Cosmic American Music.

label: Drag City
description: Hanson's first solo album away from his fuzzed-out band Wand strips things back to gentle, string-and-pedal-steel-laced folk-rock, closer to Gene Clark than to Wand's noise. His high, plaintive voice sits up front over patient, breezy arrangements. It is a quiet detour from the guitar heroics of his main band.
lineage: Moves Hanson from Wand's psych-fuzz toward a hushed country-folk sound that sounds indebted to Gene Clark and Laurel Canyon, which resurfaces in his later solo work.

label: Drag City
description: A fuller-band, more overtly country-rock record than Hanson's debut, with pedal steel and long, winding guitar solos running through desert-toned songs. It leans into the sound of vintage Neil Young and Gene Clark records without straight pastiche. It suits listeners who want wide-open, sunburnt guitar music.
lineage: Pulls Hanson's solo work closer to what sounds like classic Cosmic American Music in the Neil Young and Gene Clark mold.

label: Drag City
description: A provocatively titled record built around long guitar-solo epics, closer to Hanson's Wand side than his quieter solo debut. Country-rock tempos and pedal steel still anchor the songs even as the guitar playing stretches out at length. It suits listeners who want shredding that still feels warm and melodic.
lineage: Reconnects Hanson's solo work to long-form guitar jamming that sounds indebted to the Dead and Crazy Horse.

label: Drag City
description: A full swerve from Hanson's scorching guitar-rock records into piano-led, orchestral balladry in the Nashville Sound mold, carrying sarcastic, well-built songs. It keeps the breezy tempos of his earlier work while trading long solos for lusher, more classic-country arrangement. It is his most stylistically surprising solo record, for fans of wry, lushly dressed songcraft.
lineage: Bends Hanson's solo catalog toward orchestration that sounds indebted to the classic Nashville Sound.

label: New West Records
description: Produced by Jeff Tweedy, this album pairs the Saskatchewan cousins' antique folk repertoire and close harmonies with warmer, more electric backing than their earlier records, edging toward a breezy country-rock feel. Clayton Linthicum's fingerpicked and occasionally fuzzed guitar work sits alongside Kacy Anderson's plain, unadorned voice. It suits listeners who like old-time song forms with a gentle rock pulse.
lineage: Bridges Kacy & Clayton's traditional folk repertoire with producer Jeff Tweedy's fuller band arrangements, in a country-rock sound akin to Laurel Canyon.
borderline_note: Could also sit in V6 (classic-country revival); filed here for its country-rock production.

label: New West Records
description: A fuller-band record than The Siren's Song, with more electric guitar interplay and a breezier tempo, while keeping the duo's plainspoken, old-timey vocal delivery. It leans further from strict folk revivalism toward a country-rock sound. It suits listeners who want traditional-minded songs with a warm electric band behind them.
lineage: Extends Kacy & Clayton's move from folk repertoire toward a country-rock sound akin to Laurel Canyon.
borderline_note: Could also sit in V6; filed here for its country-rock production.

label: Self-released
description: A prolific New Jersey guitar band named for a certain Dead guitarist, this album is built around long, twin-guitar jams that move between fuzzed-out heaviness and lighter, twangy interplay. Songs regularly stretch past seven minutes, foregrounding improvisation over verse-chorus structure. It is one of the clearest examples of the 2010s Dead-revival guitar-band sound.
lineage: Directly channels the Grateful Dead's twin-guitar jam vocabulary, alongside peers like Ryley Walker and Endless Boogie in the 2010s psych-jam revival.

label: Self-released
description: A tighter, more song-focused record than Cosmic Cash, though still anchored by extended guitar interplay between the band's two lead players. Tempos loosen into breezier, more melodic territory in places, without giving up the long jams entirely. It shows the band refining rather than abandoning their Dead-indebted approach.
lineage: The band's name nods to Jerry Garcia, and its dual-guitar jamming sounds indebted to the Grateful Dead.

label: Self-released
description: A brief, folk-based debut built on plucked strings and a mallet-driven pulse, with playful, transcendental lyrics floating over spare, exploratory arrangements. The mood is spectral and cosmic, a little spooky despite its lullaby-like gentleness. It suits listeners who want hushed, spiritual folk-pop to sink into.
lineage: A hushed, folk-song take on cosmic music that sounds closer to Vashti Bunyan than to full-band jam-rock.

label: Self-released
description: Warm harmony vocals sit against loose, breezy guitar arrangements on this full-length. The songs move at an easy tempo somewhere between cosmic country and dream-pop, with fingerpicked acoustic lines and a gentle drawl. It suits listeners who like soft, sunlit harmony songwriting.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon-style harmony songwriting filtered through DIY self-release culture.

label: Self-released
description: Glyders' second full-length was flagged by Josh Terry as a forthcoming record to watch, continuing the duo's mix of breezy, harmony-driven guitar pop and cosmic-country tempos. It builds on Maria's Hunt with slightly fuller, more anthemic arrangements. The band remains a self-released Chicago project more than a decade after forming.
lineage: Continues Glyders' Laurel Canyon-indebted harmony songwriting within Chicago's independent DIY scene.

label: Full Time Hobby
description: This self-titled record blends Radiohead-style atmospherics with Nilsson-esque psychedelic pop and woozy, pub-rock-adjacent Americana. Synths and pedal steel drift together at breezy, hushed tempos. It suits listeners who like country textures pushed into dreamy, experimental pop.
lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country scene (Rich Ruth, Spencer Cullum), taken in a more song-based, psychedelic-pop direction.

label: Self-released
description: A self-released Los Angeles record built on warm, breezy guitar interplay and easygoing tempos in the Dead-revival mode. The songwriting stays understated rather than showy, favoring feel over flash.
lineage: Part of the same self-released, Dead-indebted West Coast guitar-band underground as Garcia Peoples and Cass McCombs' looser records.

label: Woodsist
description: Andrews leads this loose, sunny record of ramshackle country-folk. Ringing guitars and easygoing tempos carry conversational, unfussy songwriting throughout. It sits comfortably in the Woodsist label's twangy, DIY take on Laurel Canyon songwriting, for listeners who like their folk hazy and homespun.
lineage: Sounds akin to the hazy, harmony-driven country-folk of Woodsist labelmates Woods.
